units.title: Driving while impaired by alcohol or another drug is unlawful.
On Nebraska public roadways or public parking areas, neither a driver nor a passenger may consume alcohol or possess an open alcoholic-beverage container inside a vehicle.
Alcohol and other drugs can impair safe vehicle control and sound driving decisions.
Nebraska’s zero-tolerance alcohol rule applies to drivers younger than twenty-one.
Providing alcohol to a minor is unlawful and can create liability for resulting damage.
For a driver younger than twenty-one, a blood alcohol concentration of at least zero point zero two percent makes driving unlawful.
Driving with a blood alcohol concentration of at least zero point zero eight percent is unlawful regardless of age or vehicle type.
Violating the alcohol-driving provisions can lead to criminal penalties or administrative license revocation.
Driving on Nebraska roads constitutes agreement to chemical alcohol-or-drug testing when an officer requests it.
Refusing an officer’s request for an alcohol-or-drug test of blood, breath or urine under Nebraska’s implied-consent rule is a separate crime.
Failing, in the officer’s judgment, to complete a requested blood, breath or urine test for alcohol or drugs violates Nebraska’s implied-consent law.
Refusing a requested alcohol-or-drug chemical test under Nebraska’s implied-consent law brings a one-year administrative license revocation.
Criminal refusal penalties match the penalties for a DUI conviction involving blood alcohol concentration of at least zero point one five percent.
Depending on prior convictions, a criminal refusal conviction may revoke the license for two through fifteen years in addition to fines and jail.
Significant impairment can appear well below the general unlawful alcohol concentration of zero point zero eight percent.
Body weight is among the factors affecting alcohol absorption.
Body composition associated with sex is among the factors affecting alcohol absorption.
Food in the digestive tract is among the factors affecting alcohol absorption.
The amount of time spent drinking is among the factors affecting alcohol absorption.
A drinker who seems in control may still have seriously impaired driving ability.
Simple reaction time is impaired at a blood alcohol concentration of zero point zero four percent.
Choosing between possible responses becomes impaired beginning at a blood alcohol concentration of zero point zero three percent.
Tracking a single object becomes impaired at a blood alcohol concentration of zero point zero five percent.
Tracking several objects can be impaired at an alcohol concentration lower than that needed to impair tracking one object.
Dividing attention across tasks can be impaired below a blood alcohol concentration of zero point zero five percent.
At a blood alcohol concentration of zero point zero five percent, understanding what was seen or heard takes longer.
At a blood alcohol concentration of zero point zero five percent, eye-movement control and combining visual images decline.
Seeing detail in a moving object declines at a blood alcohol concentration of zero point zero five percent.
Hand-and-foot coordination and other precise muscular tasks are impaired at a blood alcohol concentration of zero point zero five percent.
A blood alcohol concentration of zero point zero eight percent impairs steering, braking, speed control, lane tracking, gear changes and distance judgments.
Emergency response is impaired at a blood alcohol concentration of zero point zero four percent.
If drinking is planned, arrange a designated driver or another form of transportation.
Only elapsed time reduces the body’s alcohol level and its effects.
The handbook contrasts concentration on one task at a BAC as high as zero point zero eight percent with impaired divided attention below zero point zero five percent.
A child-restraint violation carries a twenty-five-dollar fine plus court costs and one point on the operator’s record.
A general occupant-protection violation carries a twenty-five-dollar fine plus court costs.
A primary-law violation alone allows an officer to stop and ticket a driver.
A secondary-law citation requires the driver to have been stopped and ticketed for another violation.
Airbags add protection but do not replace seat-belt use.
Combining seat belts with airbags improves crash protection.
In a vehicle with a steering-wheel airbag, the recommended hand positions are nine o’clock and three o’clock.
An airbag deployment can injure children, older occupants or short adults even in a low-speed crash.
For greatest safety, children aged twelve or younger should ride in a rear seat.
Never put a rear-facing infant seat in the front passenger position of an airbag-equipped vehicle.
A driver in an airbag-equipped vehicle should leave at least ten inches between the body and steering wheel.
A child must ride rear-facing up to age two or until the child reaches the seat manufacturer’s upper height or weight limit.
Children younger than eight must be properly secured in a federally approved child safety seat.
A child younger than eight must occupy a nonfront seat when that seat has a passenger-restraint system and is not already occupied by another child younger than eight.
The under-eight child-safety-seat rule, including use of a restraint-equipped nonfront seat not already occupied by another child younger than eight, is a primary law.
Children from age eight until age eighteen must use a seat belt or child safety seat.
The restraint requirement for children aged eight through seventeen is a secondary law.
Children younger than eighteen may not ride in vehicle cargo areas.
The prohibition on children riding in cargo areas is a primary law.
All passengers must be buckled when the driver holds a provisional operator permit or a school permit.
The passenger-restraint rule for provisional or school permit drivers is a secondary law.
Child-restraint requirements apply throughout the vehicle’s seating positions.
Childcare providers must secure every child in an appropriate safety seat or seat belt.
A childcare provider’s failure to secure children can result in revocation of the childcare license.
The child-restraint requirement for childcare providers is a primary law.
Drivers and front-seat passengers must wear a seat belt or use a child safety seat.
The front-seat occupant-protection requirement also applies in autocycles.
The general driver-and-front-passenger belt requirement is a secondary law.
Never leave a child alone or unsupervised in a vehicle.
A pet left in a vehicle can suffer fatal heatstroke in minutes even when outdoor temperatures seem mild.
Do not leave pets inside a motor vehicle.
In a passenger vehicle, swerving to avoid a deer increases the risk of death or injury.
When a deer impact is imminent, brake firmly, keep steering control and stop as safely as possible.
Do not veer off the road, lose control or enter oncoming traffic to avoid a deer.
Reduce deer-crash risk by improving your view, slowing in deer-warning zones and keeping speed within headlight range.
Be alert for deer during dusk-to-dawn periods, in spring or fall, and near water or wooded areas.
After seeing a deer, look for additional deer because they travel in groups and behave unpredictably.
